tier_reason: Independent nativejson-benchmark sample CSV (miloyip, committed 2016-09-09 in a4a9f10) has taocpp/json and Nlohmann rows; harness code is public (src/tests/taocpptest.cpp, src/tests/nlohmanntest.cpp), flags are in build/premake5.lua (release optimize 'Full', -march=native), compiler (clang 7.0 64-bit, macOS) and CPU (Core i7-4980HQ) are stated in the suite README. All summed figures in the record re-derive exactly from the CSV.

corrections.workload: Parse in-memory JSON into a DOM and stringify the DOM, summed over canada.json, citm_catalog.json and twitter.json, in the nativejson-benchmark sample run of 2016-09-09 (commit a4a9f10). At that commit the thirdparty submodules point to taocpp/json d380c63 (a 2016 development commit, before the 1.0.0-beta.7 tag of 2017-05-19) and nlohmann/json c8d01fa (merge of release/2.0.3).
corrections.claimed_speedup: Parse time summed over the three files: taocpp/json 41.230 ms vs Nlohmann 72.476 ms, about 1.8x faster (derived from page data; canada 25.621 vs 55.591 ms, citm_catalog 10.266 vs 9.875 ms i.e. slightly slower there, twitter 5.343 vs 7.010 ms). Stringify summed: 30.997 ms vs 87.732 ms, about 2.8x faster (derived from page data; canada 21.560 vs 76.315, citm 6.078 vs 7.178, twitter 3.359 vs 4.239). In the same CSV RapidJSON parses the three files in 7.932 ms, so taocpp/json is about 5.2x slower than RapidJSON (derived from page data). Versions: taocpp/json submodule commit d380c63 (2016) vs Nlohmann v2.0.3; the suite README's version table lists taocpp/json 1.0.0-beta.7, but that tag postdates the CSV by eight months. taoJSON's own README makes no speed claim; it says only 'Achieves a 100% conformance score in the Native JSON Benchmark tests'.
corrections.caveats: Weak and stale. The project makes no performance claim; the evidence is a 2016-09-09 third-party shootout run by RapidJSON's author (taocpp/json at a 2016 development commit d380c63, not the 1.0.0-beta.7 the suite README's later version table names, vs Nlohmann v2.0.3), so both libraries have changed a great deal since. taocpp/json is slightly slower than Nlohmann on citm_catalog parse; the summed win comes mostly from canada.json (number-heavy). A later rerun of the same suite shown in the Sonic-Cpp README (2022 chart, hardware and versions unstated; values read off the bars, approximate) has taocpp/json parse about 5.6 ms vs Nlohmann about 6.2 ms (about 1.1x) and stringify about 2.65 vs 4.6 ms (about 1.7x), so the margin may have shrunk. Boost.JSON commit 7e72366 ('shrink sizeof(array)', doc/qbk/benchmarks.qbk) removed aggregate tao-json lines ('parse 55952763 bytes in 2178ms', 'parse 488889121 bytes in 22952ms') and added per-file nlohmann lines (1297 to 13899 ms); the two never appear in the same file version and measure different inputs, so they give no taoJSON-vs-nlohmann comparison. taocpp/json is slower than RapidJSON in every suite found. The repo has src/perf/json benchmark programs but no published comparison numbers.

notes: Numbers verified exactly against the CSV; tier A holds on the suite's public harness, premake flags, compiler and CPU. Corrected the version attribution (CSV run used taocpp/json d380c63 from 2016; 1.0.0-beta.7 was tagged 2017-05-19) and the Boost.JSON caveat (tao and nlohmann numbers there were never in the same run). Shortcomings: no first-party claim, 2016 data, slower than Nlohmann on citm_catalog parse, 5.2x slower than RapidJSON.

tier_reason: First-party bar charts only (docs/images/compare_Decode.png, compare_Encode.png, parse.png, serialize.png, all committed 2022-11-24 in c16e355); benchmark code (benchmark/ and scripts/tools/draw-decode-encode.py) and 2022 Bazel flags are public, but no CPU model or compiler is stated and the nativejson rerun was done by the Sonic authors on unstated hardware.

corrections.claimed_speedup: No figures in the README text; numbers exist only as bar charts. Values below are read off the chart images, approximate, not printed. nativejson parse chart (docs/images/parse.png, axis 0-100 ms): Sonic about 1.0 ms vs RapidJSON about 2.1 ms (about 2.2x faster), nlohmann about 6.2 ms (about 6x), taocpp/json about 5.7 ms; simdjson about 0.85 ms is faster than Sonic and YYjson about 1.1 ms is close. Serialize chart (docs/images/serialize.png, axis 0-40 ms): Sonic about 0.55 ms vs RapidJSON about 1.2 ms (about 2.2x), nlohmann about 4.6 ms (about 8x), taocpp/json about 2.65 ms, simdjson about 5.7 ms; YYjson about 0.42 ms is faster than Sonic. Own decode/encode charts normalize SonicDyn to 1.0 (higher is better): RapidJSON decode bars span about 0.16 to 0.74 (Sonic about 1.4x to 6x faster) and encode about 0.17 to 0.64; simdjson decode about 0.76 to 1.44 (above Sonic on lottie, github_events, citm_catalog and twitter, tied on canada) and encode about 0.19 to 0.49; yyjson decode about 0.68 to 1.54 (at or above Sonic on 7 of 11 files) and encode about 0.40 to 1.51 (above Sonic on 6 of 11 files).
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Charts generated in 2022 (commit c16e355) with Bazel: benchmark target copts -O3 -msse4 -Wall -Wextra -mavx2 -mbmi -mpclmul -mlzcnt -DNDEBUG -std=c++17; yyjson built with -O3 -DNDEBUG -march=haswell -g, simdjson with -O3 -DNDEBUG (bazel/*.BUILD at that commit). At HEAD the CMake path compiles bench with -O3 -DNDEBUG -g plus arch flags (Google Benchmark v1.9.5), while the Bazel benchmark target carries no -O level and scripts/tools/draw-decode-encode.py runs 'bazel build :benchmark' without --compilation_mode=opt. Compiler and version not stated.
corrections.caveats: Evidence is first-party and chart-only: no printed numbers, no CPU model, no compiler version; the y-axis label 'HIB' in the decode/encode charts is undefined (read as higher is better, normalized to SonicDyn = 1.0). All four charts date from 2022-11-24 and have not been regenerated, so they reflect late-2022 versions of Sonic, RapidJSON, yyjson and simdjson. The nativejson-benchmark chart is a rerun by the Sonic authors on unstated hardware, with libraries of unknown versions, and the Sonic adapter for that suite is not linked from the README. Sonic is not the fastest in its own charts: simdjson parses faster on the nativejson chart and on several own decode files, and yyjson serializes faster on the nativejson chart and beats Sonic on 7 of 11 decode and 6 of 11 encode files in the project's own benchmark; the clear win is over RapidJSON, nlohmann and taocpp/json. Sonic does not validate UTF-8 (README TODO 'Support validating UTF-8'), so comparisons with validating parsers such as simdjson are not like-for-like. Rerunning the chart script at HEAD (bazel build without -c opt, no -O in the benchmark target copts) would produce an unoptimized build. Requires x86 AVX2 and Linux per the README. The project's own benchmark does not include nlohmann/json.

notes: Chart readings re-checked from the PNGs and broadly match; corrected Sonic parse to about 1.0 ms and added that yyjson beats Sonic on the serialize chart and on most of Sonic's own decode/encode files. Tier C stands (no CPU or compiler). Shortcomings: chart-only 2022 first-party data, no UTF-8 validation, slower than yyjson/simdjson on many files, HEAD chart script builds without optimization.

tier_reason: First-party README table (simple_enum v0.2.0 vs magic_enum v0.9.5 and reflect) with clang 17 -ftime-trace and Ryzen 9 5900X stated and public sources in time_trace/ (simple_enum.cc, magic_enum.cc, reflect.cc, enum_definitions.h, CMakeLists.txt), but optimization/standard flags and build preset are not stated, and the largest ratio (183x) exceeds 50x with flags unstated, so it stays C.

corrections.caveats: Measures compiler frontend cost only (template instantiation time from clang -ftime-trace), not runtime lookup speed; the README gives no runtime benchmark. Numbers are for simple_enum v0.2.0 against magic_enum v0.9.5 and reflect main of 2024-02-02 (README, 2024), all since changed, and the README notes an old screenshot is from v0.0.1. Benchmark source is public (time_trace/simple_enum.cc, magic_enum.cc, reflect.cc, enum_definitions.h, CMakeLists.txt) with compiler and CPU named, so it nearly meets tier A, but optimization and standard flags and the build preset are not stated. Only bounded enums are measured: every benchmarked enum declares first/last (or adl_enum_bounds), while magic_enum.cc uses magic_enum's default value range with no enum_range or MAGIC_ENUM_RANGE customization, so magic_enum's cost is roughly constant per enum (151.590 ms for a 3-value enum) and the comparison favours the bounded case; simple_enum's unbounded mode is not measured. The README labels enum E as 15 enumerators but enum_definitions.h defines _1 to _16 (16 values). The reflect row is not comparable per the README (part of its work moves to runtime). The lead's guessed baseline (std::string_view or manual conversion) is not what is measured.

notes: All README numbers and derived ratios check out (16x, 34x, 33x, 183x); metadata (BSL-1.0, 44 stars, last commit 2026-10-01, not a fork) confirmed. Tier C stands. Shortcomings: compile-time only, bounded enums vs magic_enum's default range without range tuning, 2024 versions, flags unstated, E enumerator count mislabelled.
